https://www.thetimes.com/culture/books/a.title: How to save the world — from asteroids, supervolcanoes and AI
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/books/a.subtitle: In his lively book, The Anti-Catastrophe League, Tom Ough chronicles how scientists and tech bros are working to stop humanity from being wiped out
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/books/a.text:
On the morning of June 20, 1908, an asteroid exploded over the East Siberian taiga. “The sky split in two and fire appeared over the forest,” a witness said. “I became so hot that I couldn’t bear it, as if my shirt was on fire.” Glimpses of how the world ends are all too rare, but the Tunguska event was one. It flattened 830 square miles of forest, but killed only three people. It was the largest impact event in recorded history with a blast equivalent to about 185 Hiroshimas.
Imagine, then, the destruction if a bigger asteroid hit Earth. Even if it exploded over a similar wasteland, or in the middle of the ocean, it would cause an “impact winter”, or a mountainous tsunami. In 2004 astronomers spotted just such an asteroid, which they named Apophis after the Egyptian god of darkness and disorder. They concluded it would smite Earth on Friday 13 in April, 2029 with a blast of 100,000 or one million Hiroshimas.
That was a false alarm, but it made Nasa think: how can we stop an asteroid? Thus began Dart (Double Asteroid Redirection Test). In 2022 the Dart spacecraft was deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, a remote and unthreatening asteroid, at 13,000mph. The impact exploded enough matter to nudge the asteroid off its orbit. If we can divert Dimorphos, we could divert earthbound asteroids. “This is a watershed moment for planetary defence,” the Nasa administrator Bill Nelson said. For Tom Ough, the author of The Anti-Catastrophe League, it’s a perfect demonstration of what can be achieved when we make a concerted effort to avert catastrophe.
Tom Ough (as in, “Tom, Oh!”) is a senior editor at the website UnHerd and co-hosts the Anglofuturism podcast. (“Anglofuturism”, a term coined by the journalist Aris Roussinos, is a “right-wing progressivism … which fuses national tradition with a futuristic drive for rapid technological progress.” The Conservative MP Robert Jenrick claims to be an Anglofuturist.)
His podcast’s quaintly galactic vision of Britain includes “Georgian townhouses on the moon, the highest GDP per capita in the Milky Way [and] small modular reactors under every village green” while casting a rapacious eye towards the mineral riches of the British Antarctic Territory.
The Anti-Catastrophe League is a consummate and thorough exploration of “catastrophic risks” and “extinction risks” (“those being the academic terms for things that might kill lots of us and things that might kill all of us”) and the heroes trying to prevent them. They are a “diffuse team” of computer scientists, engineers, “effective altruists” and thanatophobes. At parties, some cheerily trade their “p(doom) numbers” with self-importance — those being the probability each places on humanity’s extinction coming soon.
How, then, does it all end? Possibly via super-volcanoes, solar storms, a lab-leaked pandemic, nuclear war, climate change, electromagnetic-pulse attacks or artificial intelligence. Remember the chaos — 100,000 flights cancelled — caused in 2010 by the Icelandic volcano Eyjafjallajokull. That volcano is a minnow compared with the 20 or so super-volcanoes that exist. An eruption by one of those could be 100,000 times bigger than that event. The last super-volcanic eruption was Toba in Indonesia 74,000 years ago, and some anthropologists have calculated that Toba reduced the world’s human population to about 10,000.
• What we’re reading this week — by the Times books team
Several of these super-volcanoes loom over the Malacca straits, through which about 40 per cent of global trade passes. But if one erupted, it is the attendant earthquake and tsunami we will need look out for. In which case, Ough writes, “One hopes that the Singaporean laboratory that handles some of the world’s deadliest pathogens is prepared for flooding.” It probably isn’t.
Stoppering super-volcanoes, however, will soon be possible. One paper from Nasa suggests placing geothermal systems beside Yellowstone’s magma chamber, which — over 50,000 years — would cool the volcano while generating competitively priced electricity. But, naturally, “there are legal and technical obstacles”. There are also moral objections. “Many people feel intuitively that planetary systems should be sacrosanct,” Ough says. He is frequently maddened by humankind’s nimby aversion to “playing God”.
Chances are, though, our extinction will be self-inflicted. Or else, as crafty as humanity seems, artificial general intelligence will be craftier. To think AI would kill us gradually is stupid, the philosopher and Harry Potter fan-fiction author Eliezer Yudkowsky says. More likely is that it “build[s] itself a tiny molecular laboratory and manufacturer[s] and release[s] lethal bacteria — which would look like everybody falling over dead inside the same second.”
The AI would then carpet the planet with data centres and solar panels and plod along solitudinously until the universe’s eventual heat death. Unsurprisingly, Yudkowsky thinks we should stop developing general purpose AI. However, the chief executive officer of OpenAI, Sam Altman — who thinks a “lights out for all of us” scenario is possible — keeps pushing ahead.
More cheerily, tackling climate change might trigger limitless economic growth. Ough is an apostle for nuclear energy — “we could make a Scottish winter bearable, or an Arabian summer temperate. We could irrigate deserts, bringing life and greenery to arid wilderness.” Ough is at his best when straining towards a science-fictional utopia that’s almost graspable.
“Our belief is that by the standards of the future our energy consumption today, and therefore our standard of living, remains abysmally low,” say the engineer Austin Vernon and the economist Eli Dourado, believers in the superabundant energy possibility of more nuclear power. But nuclear power is often thwarted by the “Pro-Catastrophe League”, a Satanic cabal consisting of Just Stop Oil activists, the Greens in Germany, nimbys and “the architects of [Britain’s] planning regime”.
• Read more book reviews and interviews — and see what’s top of the Sunday Times Bestsellers List
In the distant future, Ough suggests, we could even harness black holes for energy, but for now there’s supercritical water, found deep within the Earth, which is “water pressurised and heated beyond 373C, at which point it has … an energy density not far off from that of fossil fuels.” Such things as the possibility of geothermal energy exist beyond my natural curiosities, but Ough’s explanations are so accessible as to make me share in his enthusiasm. He can be winsomely dorkish: as a “geothermal fanboy”, he writes, “the blood runs hot in my veins as I imagine supercritical fluid gushing through the pipes of converted oil and gas infrastructure.”
Of course, this is all worthless if we can’t surmount the final obstacle — biological death. Ough speaks to scientists who believe in the possibility of uploading our brains to a computer, then recreating them (whole-brain emulation) or the “singularity” when humanity merges with super-intelligent AI. But maybe even biological death can be put off. The computer scientist turned gerontologist Aubrey de Grey says “the first human to live to 1,000 has already been born” and he believes in the “Methuselarity” whereby new anti-ageing therapies mean we will live long enough to benefit from future ones.
That quest for immortality reveals what motivates Ough’s league: a need to overcome our little lives and vanquish death. “Being brave/ Let’s no one off the grave,” Philip Larkin once wrote. Ough, though, seems to think it could. “Our destiny, for better or worse, seems rather malleable,” he writes. “The shape it will take is ours to choose.”
The Anti-Catastrophe League: The Pioneers and Visionaries on a Quest to Save the World by Tom Ough (Mudlark £22 pp336). To order a copy go to timesbookshop.co.uk. Free UK standard P&P on orders over £25. Special discount available for Times+ members.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.title: UN climate ruling ushers in fresh hopes of accountability
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.subtitle: Critics point out that causation will be difficult for states to prove if they try to sue those they blame for the harm caused by global warming
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.text:
Companies may face tougher regulations in the wake of the UN court’s landmark climate change ruling, but polluted states are likely to face an uphill battle for compensation.
Environmental groups, small island nations and other climate change campaigners welcomed last week’s “advisory opinion” from the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in the Netherlands, which said that countries were obliged under the climate change treaty regime and customary international law to protect the environment from greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and limit global warming.
States that breach these obligations may be required to cease their wrongful conduct, offer guarantees of non-repetition and pay compensation to those affected. The court affirmed that climate change is an urgent and existential threat that is “unequivocally caused by human activities”.
Giving the ruling, the court’s president, Iwasawa Yuji, a judge from Japan, said that a “failure of a state to take appropriate action to protect the climate system from GHG emissions — including through fossil fuel production, fossil fuel consumption, the granting of fossil fuel exploration licences or the provision of fossil fuel subsidies — may constitute an internationally wrongful act which is attributable to that state”.
The judgment came after a fortnight of evidence sessions in December in what was something of a bonanza for a fleet of British barristers — including Cherie Blair KC — who acted for countries such as Tuvalu, the Maldives, Belize, Namibia and Ghana. Blair represented Albania and Sir Michael Wood KC represented Saudi Arabia.
For the UK, the attorney-general, Lord Hermer KC, said that he understood the “pressing, urgent need for the world to tackle climate change” and the “frustration expressed” by campaigners that some countries were not doing enough to do so.
• UN climate ruling ‘flawed’ and reparations unnecessary, minister says
However, Hermer argued against imposing legal obligations on countries that go beyond the Paris agreement — a legally binding treaty on cutting the greenhouse gas emissions that drive climate change. Hermer described that agreement as containing “robust obligations that meaningfully address protection of the climate system” and representing “the most relevant applicable international instrument for addressing the challenge”.
The case is part of a trend in rulings from international courts around climate issues, including last year when the International Court of Human Rights ruled that the Swiss government’s climate policies violated human rights.
Although the UN court’s ruling is not binding, experts suggest it could have wide-ranging consequences, opening the way for vulnerable countries to sue those they blame for the harm caused by global warming.
The opinion “is the start of a new era of climate accountability at a global level” that “marks a turning point for climate justice”, says Danilo Garrido, legal counsel at Greenpeace International.
• Band of female eco activists win landmark climate case
But one practical difficulty for campaigners aiming to rely on the ruling, notes Andrew Denny, a partner at A&O Shearman, is that a state can only bring proceedings against another if both have agreed to resolve such disputes before the ICJ. And while countries such as the UK have agreed to submit to its jurisdiction, America and China have not.
In addition, Denny says, the court has drawn a distinction between injured and non-injured states. “Injured states may claim compensation, while non-injured states can only seek for a polluting state to cease its wrongful act and guarantee non-repetition,” he says.
If a state is seeking monetary compensation for breaches of climate change obligations, it must demonstrate that it has suffered injury resulting from the actions of the other state, he explains, which may present difficulties in proving causation and loss, particularly when the alleged injury results from omissions rather than direct actions.
Establishing causation between greenhouse gas emissions and specific climate-related harm is “factually complex and legally challenging”, says Fabrice Mattei, a lawyer at the firm Rouse, which “may significantly limit the practical impact of the ICJ’s opinion”.
Mattei explains that while scientific progress now allows experts to link certain extreme weather events or temperature anomalies to greenhouse gas emissions, courts require a much higher evidentiary threshold. Demonstrating that a company’s or state’s action caused the harm, Mattei suggests, is likely to be difficult, particularly as the climate impact is rarely the result of greenhouse gas emissions alone.
States can attempt to bring cases before national domestic courts, but those judges might impose strict legal standing requirements that restrict those who are entitled to bring claims to directly injured parties.
• China floods: 80,000 evacuated in Beijing as at least 38 killed
Most international courts require both parties to consent before they will hear cases — and countries such as the US and China are unlikely to accept jurisdiction or participate in proceedings. Any actions, Mattei suggests, are likely to face “significant political resistance and institutional reluctance”, adding that interstate litigation is “politically sensitive and countries may fear diplomatic backlash, economic consequences, or retaliation”.
Even where a judgment is obtained, enforcing reparations or specific climate actions, he suggests, would be difficult without political will or treaty mechanisms.
To bring an action against the UK, the retired Supreme Court judge Lord Sumption explains, a state would have to show that the county was in breach of the obligations set out by the ICJ. He suggests that is “not at all self-evident”, explaining that “we have signed up to the Paris agreement, we’re not in breach of it, we’ve accepted what the international climate change panel of the United Nations recommends, which is net zero by 2050”.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.title: Palestine Action activist wore £6,000 gown to debutante ball
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.subtitle: Georgie Robertson, 32, the daughter of Kathy Lette, the author, and Geoffrey Robertson KC, the human rights lawyer, has gone from Cannes to the courts
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
The Crillon Ball is described by Tatler as the “world’s most glamorous debutante ball”. Georgie Robertson came out to society in a £6,000 gown, alongside Princess Diana’s niece Lady Kitty Spencer, and boasted afterwards of a “fairytale event in which the aristocracy rub sequinned shoulder pads with the celebritocracy”.
Fast forward to 2025 and the 32-year-old daughter of Kathy Lette, the author, and Geoffrey Robertson KC, the human rights lawyer, has swapped pearls for protest.
The former Labour press officer under Jeremy Corbyn was helping Palestine Action with its press coverage as it fought being proscribed by the government in court.
Her spell volunteering for the pro-Palestinian protest group is the latest twist in a life that her mother joked went “from one extreme to the other, from Marxism to Marie Antoinette”.
In an article written after the Crillon Ball in 2009, Robertson said the weekend in Paris was “an endless flurry of hot hair rollers, make-up, trying on diamonds, couture fittings and fashion shoots” — which included posing for Tatler.
She recounted having “shared giggles and gossip” with Clint Eastwood’s daughter, an Indian princess, Lady Kitty Spencer and Angelica Hicks, the great-granddaughter of Lord Mountbatten.
Other society outings included the Elle Style Awards and the UK premiere of Blue Jasmine, starring Cate Blanchett, in 2013.
Robertson was schooled at the private Queen’s College in central London. She stood for election as women’s officer for the London Young Labour committee, pledging to “work with grassroots women’s campaigns to collectively organise against patriarchy and all other forms of oppression”.
She went on to work in Corbyn’s office when he was leader of the opposition, before being elected as a Labour councillor in Camden, north London.
After Sir Keir Starmer became leader, the Labour Party pursued Robertson and several other Corbyn-era staff with legal action, accusing them of leaking a report about antisemitism in the party to the press. The case was dropped in 2024.
Social media shows Robertson continues to mix with celebrities such as Tim Minchin, the comic and composer, and Kylie Minogue.
She also attended the Cannes film festival.
Weeks later, during a hearing at the Royal Courts of Justice as Palestine Action fought its proscription, she posted a photo on Instagram showing Mr Justice Chamberlain being addressed by a barrister acting for the group, with the caption: “Nearly 9 hours so far, waiting with baited breath.” It is a criminal offence to take photographs inside a courtroom.
Less than 24 hours later, she continued to brief journalists on the activities of Defend Our Juries, a left-wing pressure group that has launched a campaign of civil disobedience against Palestine Action’s proscription, calling it an “Orwellian nightmare”.
The campaign has led to the arrest of dozens of protesters for holding signs that read “I support Palestine Action”.
An escalating series of protests is being supported by Palestine Action’s founder Huda Ammori, who told 1,000 supporters that organised civil disobedience “will make the ban unenforceable”.
Defend Our Juries was set up by Tim Crosland, a former government lawyer who was debarred for leaking court documents.
• Police defend arrest of 83-year-old Palestine Action activist
Over the last two Saturdays, police have made over 100 arrests under terror laws after the group co-ordinated sit-in protests around the country. Dozens more are expected on Saturday in Parliament Square in London, Bristol, Edinburgh, Manchester and Truro in Cornwall.
The protesters, who held signs that read “I support Palestine Action”, risked prison as the direct action group was banned under the Terrorism Act from July 5.
Crosland said he hoped the protests will “expose the absurdity” of the proscription.
In a briefing for activists taking part in the protests last week, Crosland said the ban “is like something out of George Orwell, it’s a mad insult to the intelligence of us all”. He added: “As long as we turn up in numbers we expose this.”
Crosland set up Defend Our Juries to protest the treatment of environmental activists in trials and to push jurors to acquit defendants according to their conscience.
He was called to the bar in 1994 and worked as a criminal defence barrister, which included representing death row inmates on appeal in New Orleans.
He became deputy director of the Serious Organised Crime Agency (Soca) and head of cyber and information law at the National Crime Agency, which replaced it. He was then head of legal at the National Criminal Intelligence Service.
He later became director of Plan B, an environmental campaign group. In 2020, Crosland was found guilty of contempt of court and fined £5,000 for leaking an embargoed Supreme Court ruling about the third Heathrow runway on Twitter.
Before his contempt hearing, Crosland said: “If fighting for my children’s lives makes me a criminal, then so be it.” The judges ruled there is “no such thing as a justifiable contempt of court”.
In 2023, Crosland was disbarred by an independent disciplinary tribunal, following charges of professional misconduct brought by the Bar Standards Board.
The group claims protesters who are on remand or in prison for causing a public nuisance or criminal damage are “political prisoners” and has previously counted Chris Packham and Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall among its supporters.
A notable protest was held outside the appeal at the High Court in London in January of 16 Just Stop Oil activists who had shut down the M25. About 1,000 Defend Our Juries activists blocked the street.
An open letter co-ordinated by the group was signed by the former Archbishop of Canterbury, Rowan Williams, as well as Sandi Toksvig, the television presenter, and Danny Boyle, the director.
The group was also critical when courts barred defendants from making political arguments in their defence, claiming this kept “the truth” from jurors.
When climate protests folded under the weight of new police powers and tough sentencing, Defend Our Juries turned its attention towards Gaza.
Defend Our Juries was associatied with Palestine Action before its ban, having signed a “statement of solidarity” in November last year.
The protests over the last two weekends have been organised on the encrypted messaging apps Signal and Telegram, with online briefings given to hundreds of potential participants on Zoom.
Each person is directed towards carefully prepared briefing notes online, and handed signs and so-called “bust cards” with solicitors’ details in case of arrest.
Those involved in the protests include activists who were repeatedly arrested in the Extinction Rebellion and Just Stop Oil campaigns.

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/the-tim.title: Palestine Action is malign, but terror status goes too far
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/the-tim.text:
At midnight on Saturday, Palestine Action ­became officially proscribed under the Terrorism Act. In that ignoble status, it joins al-Qaeda, Hamas and Isis. Voicing support for, or being a member of, Palestine Action is now punishable by up to 14 years in prison. Predictably enough, a number of adherents of the anti-Israeli direct action group do not seem to have been chastened. Following a failed last-minute High Court effort to block the group’s proscription, dozens of protestors were arrested over the weekend on suspicion of supporting the organisation. They included an 83-year-old priest, as well as others thought to be “wearing clothing or displaying articles” ­indicating membership of a terrorist organisation.
That Palestine Action is a malign force is ­beyond doubt. Its members include sinister ­ideologues, deeply confused in their geopolitical outlooks and their assessment of the best way to secure their objectives. The group’s “disruptive tactics” involve calculated acts of criminal damage, illegal occupation of premises, and intimidating acts of vandalism. Since its founding in 2020, the group has had a hand in around 500 distinct instances of “direct action”, often targeting firms and property suspected of having links to Israel. The most serious act for which the group claimed credit was when four people were arrested on ­suspicion of causing £7 million of damage to two military transporter aircraft at RAF Brize Norton. It was this that prompted Yvette Cooper, the home secretary, to judge that the group had “crossed the threshold established in the Terrorism Act”.
• Police defend arrest of 83-year-old Palestine Action activist
Yet, however wanton its criminality, it remains a stretch to brand Palestine Action a terror group. Its members are qualitatively different from those of al-Qaeda, and pose a substantially different kind of threat to public order and national security. Their tactics more closely ­resemble those of extremist environmentalist groups like Just Stop Oil and Extinction Rebellion than those of ­Islamist terrorists. In recent months, a combination of public ill will, effective prosecution and proportionate sentencing have made it unviable for climate activists to persist with their criminal antics. In March this year, Just Stop Oil ­announced an end to its practices of criminal vandalism, claiming implausibly to have achieved its objectives. In reality, they were prosecuted into submission by legitimate use of the criminal law.
The heavy-handed branding of Palestine Action as terrorists risks seeming absurd when ­bona fide hostile military groupings like the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps remain ­unproscribed. The destruction of property that Palestine Action has made its calling card can already be prosecuted.
There are legitimate ­concerns that such measures risk suppressing ­dissent on the part of those politically opposed to the ­government’s support of Israeli defence policy. Palestine Action’s members may be misguided, but Britain must remain a country in which the right to express unpopular and dissenting political views is not subject to outright prohibition.
The emergence in recent years of activist groups that make criminal forms of destruction and public nuisance their modus operandi does raise challenges for law enforcement. Lord Walney, the government’s former independent adviser on ­extremism, has recently mooted an amendment to the Crime and Policing Bill which would give police greater power to curb the illegal antics of extremist groups that fall shy of terrorist organisations. These might include powers to block their ability to fundraise, organise on social media, or live-stream acts of criminality.
These lighter-touch measures would be an obviously apt ­response to the level of threat posed. Palestine Action are an antisocial menace to public order; but politicians should not do them the service of taking them as seriously as they take themselves.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Turnberry locals on Trump: We love ‘Big Donald’ and his $50 tips
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.subtitle: Donald Trump will stop by his Scottish golf courses on a ‘private visit’ this weekend. Despite the protests, many Ayrshire residents are happy to see him
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Taking the temperature from the placards during President Trump’s last visit to Scotland — variations of “Scotland against Trump” and “Trump go home” — it might seem like the country is bitterly against the president.
Yet to Turnberry, a small seaside town in South Ayrshire, it is the protesters who are the real enemy, damaging property and hijacking headlines.
The residents in the area surrounding Trump Turnberry, the first golf course the president will visit this weekend, have described their support for “Big Donald”, who once gave staff $50 tips and invited neighbours to coffee.
Irene Wright, 66, a retired council worker from Glasgow, has spent her holidays at her caravan in Maidens for the last ten years.
“I hope they don’t do all these protests because I’ll be raging,” she said, “ I want him welcomed. I like Big Donald.”
Wright praised his immigration policies, adding her fury about the Greenpeace activist who had paraglided over the golf course in 2018 “threatening” Trump from above.
“I just don’t like that it’s portrayed that Scotland doesn’t welcome him, because a lot of people do and it’s the same all over Britain,” she said.
The White House has described Trump’s visit as a “private” trip, visiting his businesses, before an official state visit in September.
• Trump’s links to Scotland — from golf courses to family history
Angela Bryce, 50, who has lived in neighbouring Maidens since April, said the protesters should leave Trump to his holiday.
“How bad is it that that man can’t just go like any normal human being and play golf? Look what he’s sacrificed to help others,” she said.
“Everything he does is positive. I mean, look at these people — they’re getting employed now because he’s here.”
Trump bought the Turnberry golf course and hotel in 2014, saving it from what one local described as the threat of “rack and ruin”. Most locals know a family or friend who is employed by the resort.
Tam Cuthill, 63, from Kirkoswald, worked as a greenkeeper at Turnberry for 38 years, retiring in 2017.
“It’s one of them ones, it’s 50/50, you either love or hate him,” he said, adding that it was the workers who were most impacted by Palestine Action spray-painting the entrance signs and poisoning grass on the green. “Staff lost hours because they had to shut the hotel,” he said, shaking his head.
Cuthill was at Turnberry when Trump bought it.
“The first thing that happened when he came — it was the Women’s Open — he stopped them playing while he came on and did his thing at the 11th green and he shook our hands and gave us all $50,” Cuthill said.
“I never found anything wrong with him as such, we complained more about some of his right-hand men. From their point of view, they wanted to be seen as authoritative in his presence.
“He certainly didn’t commit to saying anything bad or anything like that, he’s more likely to shake your hand.”
Residents near Menie in Aberdeenshire, where Trump built his first Scottish golf course, have been vocal against his development, refusing to sell him their land and one flying a Mexican flag outside his home in protest. In Turnberry, however, even those who have disagreed with Trump speak favourably of him.
Christina and David Auld, who have lived in a house neighbouring the fourth tee for 32 years, declined an offer from Trump to sell their land to him.
“We thought we were just being invited up for coffee, didn’t we dear?” Christina said, adding that he drank a Coke with sweeteners. The couple did not want to sell their home.
• Trump security leaves Turnberry ‘looking like an American prison’
“He was fine,” she said, about their refusal, “and he said at the end of it, ‘I hope we can still remain friends because we’re neighbours.’ He invited us to the opening of the hotel, the opening of the golf course.”
“The last time he was here, we just sat up in the bedroom and watched him teeing off,” she added, joking that they should invite him round for tea.
Slightly further up the road lies a National Trust attraction, the 18th-century home of Souter Johnnie, immortalised by Robert Burns in the poem Tam o’ Shanter. Souter’s Inn, the restaurant, bar and ice cream shop nearby, regularly serves Turnberry guests.
Eric Trump, the president’s son whom staff described as a “lovely guy” but “quiet”, also eats there on his frequent visits to Turnberry.
A staff member at Souter’s Inn said she always spoke to golfers about Trump.
“I’m a fan. I think he says it how it is,” she said, “He’s very good to staff as well, I’ve heard good reviews from staff members, especially during Covid times as well. They say he always gives them personal tips.
“There’s obviously the unfortunate haters, like when the golf course was damaged the last time. There’s no need for that.”
A bar staff member added, “A lot of people round here would be anti-protesters because obviously they couldn’t get jobs for weeks.
“It’s meant to be his baby, that hotel is. He wants the Open there. Even the golfers would prefer it there because the golf is supposedly the best in Scotland.”
Despite the praise for Trump’s investment, many residents were indifferent to Trump’s visit. One resident described the president as “uncouth”, another said he speaks with a “childish vocabulary”.
“The main problem is because it’s a private thing, it’s not a state visit,” one local said, “It’s a holiday for him and it’s costing millions, as if he’s not got enough money, he could have paid for it himself.”
